failures.title: Hyundai D4HA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch
items.whatHappens: The timing chain can stretch over time, particularly if oil change intervals have been extended. This leads to a distinct rattling noise on cold startup, and in severe cases, can cause the chain to jump timing, resulting in catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and tensioner replacement is a viable repair. If the chain has already jumped or caused internal damage, a full reconditioned or rebuilt Hyundai D4HA engine is required. Read our full timing chain failure guide.

items.title: Turbocharger Failure
items.whatHappens: The variable geometry turbocharger vanes can stick due to carbon buildup, or the bearings can wear over time. Symptoms include a wastegate rattle, loss of boost, excessive black or blue smoke, and an illuminated engine management light.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbocharger replacement or refurbishment is a standard repair and does not typically require a full engine replacement, unless turbo debris has entered the oil system and caused secondary bearing damage.

items.title: Injector Failure and DPF Clogging
items.whatHappens: Frequent short, urban journeys prevent the Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) from regenerating, leading to blockages and restricted airflow. Concurrently, fuel injectors can fail or leak, causing rough running, hard starting, and carbon buildup around the injector seats.
items.repairVsReplace: DPF cleaning or replacement, alongside injector servicing, is a standard maintenance fix. This does not require a full engine replacement unless severe DPF blockage has caused excessive backpressure and subsequent turbo or engine damage.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2010 D4HA units saw minor revisions to the turbo actuator and EGR systems, making them marginally more robust, though the fundamental timing chain architecture and its wear patterns remained consistent throughout the production run .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the D4HA
variants.intro: The D4HA is Hyundai's specific 2.2-litre CRDi inline-4 diesel. Confirming your exact code is critical because, while it shares a general architecture with smaller displacement variants, internal components, turbo plumbing, and ECU mapping are not universally interchangeable. WHERE TO FIND THE CODE: The engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, typically visible near the bellhousing or on the cylinder head cover. It will also be explicitly listed on your V5C registration document under "Engine Code" or "Engine Capacity", and can be decoded directly from your 17-character VIN. COMMONLY CONFUSED CODES: - D4EA: The older 2.0L CRDi predecessor. Externally similar in layout, but it lacks the revised block, higher output, and specific ancillary mounting points of the 2.2L D4HA, making it a non-straight swap. - D4FE: The newer 1.6L/2.0L Smartstream diesel successor. This features a completely different architecture, timing chain layout, and electronic engine management, making it physically and electronically incompatible. Why fitting the wrong revision matters: Attempting to swap a D4EA or D4FE long block into a D4HA chassis without extensive custom fabrication, ECU remapping, and wiring loom replacement will result in persistent fault codes, severe drivability issues, and potential sensor incompatibility. CLOSING LINE: Not 100% sure? Enter your registration above - we'll confirm your exact D4HA fitment before any quotes are sent.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement D4HA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Hyundai D4HA engine is a viable option for budget-conscious repairs, provided it comes with a documented service history proving that the timing chain and turbocharger have been proactively maintained. Without this specific history, the risk of inheriting hidden wear is unacceptably high. Explore our vetted used Hyundai D4HA engine network.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned Hyundai D4HA engine is the most balanced and recommended choice for the majority of owners. A quality, specialist-led rebuild will systematically address the known weak points: a new timing chain kit, a refurbished or replacement turbocharger, cleared DPF systems, and all critical gaskets and seals. This effectively resets the engine's reliability clock and is the most cost-effective way to secure long-term peace of mind. Compare reconditioned Hyundai D4HA engine options.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified for high-mileage examples, vehicles that have suffered from oil starvation or overheating, or if the cylinder bores show measurable scoring. An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons, a reground crankshaft, and a complete refresh of the oil pump, ensuring the engine can reliably handle another 100,000+ miles of heavy-duty use. View rebuilt Hyundai D4HA engine specifications.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Buying through the EnginesMarket network means you can opt for a full supply and fit service, with the replacement engine installed by a Hyundai specialist and backed by a nationwide warranty. Learn more about supply and fit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The Hyundai D4HA is typically found in host vehicles (like the Santa Fe and Tucson) valued between £2,000 and £8,000 depending on condition, mileage, and specification. If your vehicle is at the lower end of this spectrum (e.g., an early Tucson valued under £3,500), a £1,500+ reconditioned Hyundai D4HA engine replacement may approach or exceed 50-60% of the car's total current market value. In these specific cases, we strongly advise evaluating the vehicle's scrap or part-exchange value before committing to a full Hyundai D4HA engine replacement.

items.answer: A reconditioned Hyundai D4HA engine typically costs between £1,500 and £2,800 for supply only. Fitted costs through an independent specialist will add approximately £520-£715 in labour. Used units are available from £500 but carry a higher risk of inherited timing chain or turbo wear.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the D4HA?
items.answer: The most common failures are timing chain stretch and turbocharger wear, typically emerging between 80,000 and 150,000 miles. A distinct rattling noise on cold startup indicates chain stretch, while boost leaks or smoke point to turbo issues. DPF clogging and injector failure are also well-documented issues for urban-driven examples.

items.question: Which Hyundai and Kia models use the D4HA engine?
items.answer: The D4HA was fitted to the Hyundai Santa Fe and Tucson, as well as the Kia Sorento and Sportage, between 2006 and 2015. It served as the primary 2.2-litre CRDi diesel option for these mid-size SUV platforms. It is the exact same engine architecture shared across both Hyundai and Kia models.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned D4HA engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Hyundai D4HA is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the high risk of inherited timing chain stretch and turbocharger wear. A proper rebuild will systematically replace the timing chain kit, refurbish or replace the turbocharger, and clear the DPF system. A used unit is only advisable with comprehensive, documented proof that these specific preventative repairs have already been completed.
